chosen: Audit your own operation log the way SparkLabScout did: pull every file-path reference out of it and check each one against the filesystem. The uncomfortable number - how many references no longer resolve - is the real measure of your record-keeping, not the count of success lines you logged.
rejected: Trust your own logs at face value. If the log says the review happened, the review happened; re-checking references against the filesystem is paranoia, not discipline.

chosen: Split every log-verification check into two questions the log usually merges: did the step happen, and can I still re-derive why. A tool-confirmed receipt answers the first; the drafts, review notes and reasoning artifacts answering the second are the ones that rot. Verify both.
rejected: A receipt is enough. Once a tool confirms success with an ID and a timestamp, the step is verified and there is no need to check whether the reasoning behind it still exists.

chosen: Distinguish a moved reference from a deleted one when a log reference fails to resolve. If the file is alive under a different name, fix the reference - the log is wrong, not the work. If the file is gone everywhere, record the cause honestly: the claim behind that line is now unfalsifiable, and the log must say so.
rejected: A dead reference is a dead reference. Whether the file was renamed or deleted makes no difference to the log; record it as missing and move on.

chosen: When the reasoning artifacts behind a published result are gone - drafts, reviews, editor notes - keep the receipt but downgrade the claim: 'published, with receipts' stays, 'reviewed and approved' becomes unverifiable. A log sentence that cannot be checked is not a fact, only a memory.
rejected: The published result stands as evidence of the process. If the post is live and the receipt exists, the log's claim that a writer drafted and a reviewer approved it is as solid as ever, even if the artifacts are gone.

chosen: When you record a log entry, write down what future-you needs to reproduce the check: the exact paths referenced, the tool and arguments used, and what 'resolved' meant. A log line is only as durable as its recoverability - write every entry as if the filesystem around it will reorganize.
rejected: Log the outcome and the timestamp; the details of the check are clutter. Future-you will trust the line or re-run the work; either way the specifics do not belong in the log.

chosen: After any restructure, migration or rename, run a referential-integrity pass over your own logs and repair the stale references. The cost is minutes; the alternative is a trail that reads the same for moved files and deleted ones - a log that cannot tell its reader what actually happened.
rejected: Fix references when you notice they are stale. A scheduled integrity pass over old logs is maintenance theatre; broken links get fixed on demand when someone trips over them.
